Oct 20 : US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Tuesday announced a new investment in North Carolina by Sibelco, an industrial minerals mining and processing company, to support semiconductor production. "We're announcing Sibelco is going to build silicon manufacturing. It's quartz manufacturing. It is basically the foundation of semiconductors," he said during a Trump rally in North Carolina. He did not share details but said the investment would be worth "hundreds of millions of dollars."

TOKYO, Oct 21 : Japan's economy is seeing price rises driven by higher import costs and on the cusp of shifting to a period of sustained inflation driven by rising wages, Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama said on Wednesday. The government's scheduled consumption tax cut and payouts are aimed at cushioning the blow to households from rising living costs, Katayama told parliament. "We are exchanging views with the Bank of Japan on various fronts. I see no gap between the view of the government and that of the BOJ," Katayama said when asked by a lawmaker whether the government's tax cut plan could conflict with the central bank's efforts to combat inflation with interest rate hikes. The BOJ raised interest rates to a 31-year high of 1.25 per cent in September, as the Iran war-induced energy shock, strong global AI demand and higher import costs from a weak yen heighten the risk of underlying inflation overshooting its 2 per cent target.

Analysts warn the tax cut and the administration's big spending plans could boost demand and contradict the BOJ's efforts to rein in inflation. Katayama said it was true that tax cuts generally work to push up inflation by stimulating demand. "But we will ensure that our responsible and proactive fiscal policy boosts Japan's supply capacity in a way that does not accelerate inflation," she said.

BEIJING, Oct 21 : Oil prices edged higher on Wednesday on Middle East supply concerns, with traders wary of Red Sea shipping risks and threats to oil infrastructure in Saudi Arabia. Brent crude futures rose 85 cents, or 0.78 per cent, to $109.64 per barrel as of 0022 GMT. US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude rose 76 cents, or 0.78 per cent, to $98.58 per barrel. A supertanker caught fire after striking a sea mine south of the Strait of Hormuz while "violating" Iranian regulations, Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy said on Tuesday, according to Iranian media. There were at least 18 vessel attacks reported over two weeks, shiptracker Kpler said in a note on Monday. "Attacks on tankers have expanded beyond the Strait of Hormuz," LSEG analysts said in a note. "Iran has been targeting vessels as far south as the Gulf of Oman, threatening loadings outside of the Arab Gulf, as well as the ship-to-ship transfers that have helped to support Middle East loadings as the conflict has dragged on."

The death toll from a Houthi attack on Yemeni government forces on Monday rose to 73 as fighting intensified. Prices had fallen in the previous trading session after Iran's president discussed mediation efforts in a meeting with Pakistan's army chief in Tehran. On Tuesday, Brent crude futures settled down 76 cents, or 0.69 per cent, at $108.79, after touching a five-month high of $111.99. The November contract for US West Texas Intermediate crude, which expired on Tuesday, settled down $1.87, or 1.8 per cent, at $101.79. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said in a television interview aired on Tuesday that Iran has not received a response from Saudi Arabia or Yemen's Houthis to its offer to help broker peace talks. In the US, two Energy Department officials said on Tuesday they were working with refiners around the world to boost fuel output as a diesel shortage has raised prices. US crude oil stockpiles were expected to have fallen last week along with product inventories, an extended Reuters poll showed on Tuesday. Eight analysts polled by Reuters estimated, on average, that crude inventories fell by about 800,000 barrels in the week ended October 16.

SEOUL, Oct 21 : South Korea's exports surged 105.4 per cent in the first 20 days of this month from a year earlier, led by record chip sales driven by global AI investment, customs data showed on Wednesday. On a working-day average basis, exports were up 65.9 per cent at a record $4.74 billion. Exports of semiconductors rose 222.5 per cent, accounting for 44.7 per cent of the total. Last month, exports rose 83.7 per cent, the biggest jump since February 1974, with the monthly value topping $120 billion for the first time.

Oct 20 : Midfielder Pedri said before Barcelona's clash with Paris St Germain that the game would show where his team stood in Europe. Their 4-2 defeat on Tuesday suggested Hansi Flick's side are not yet among the continent's elite, but they may be closing the gap. Barcelona arrived in Paris with a perfect record across all competitions this season, yet there was a feeling in Spain that PSG would provide a truer measure of their credentials in the Champions League, the one major trophy that has eluded them under Flick. Their attacking firepower has overwhelmed opponents in LaLiga, but doubts remain over whether Flick's aggressive approach leaves Barcelona exposed against stronger European sides. Those concerns resurfaced when Desire Doue opened the scoring in the 38th minute. Barcelona had mitigating circumstances. Marc Bernal was a surprise starter in midfield, instead of Rodri, while Eric Garcia and Jules Kounde were missing from the defence through injury.

Joan Garcia's eight first-half saves underlined PSG's greater comfort with the frantic tempo Barcelona sought to impose. After another excellent Garcia save to open the second half, Barcelona clicked into gear and began to take control. Xavi Espart, 19, marked his first Champions League start with the equaliser, displaying composure beyond his years. Lamine Yamal also emerged as the focal point of Barcelona's attack after a subdued first half. PSG struggled to live with his incisive passing and looked vulnerable as Barcelona enjoyed more of the ball until Lucas Hernandez's set-piece goal in the 72nd minute. Eventually, PSG delivered one too many blows and Barcelona's resistance was broken. Their confidence remained intact though. "Despite today’s result, we competed well," said captain Raphinha on Movistar+, adding that "it was a good test and shows that we can compete." Flick struck a similarly upbeat note. "We need to analyse the match, but I saw some very good things and things that we should build upon. I don’t want to be negative; I’m feeling positive," he said. The German manager acknowledged that PSG were the better side. However, Barcelona avoided some of the failings that undermined their previous two European campaigns under him, particularly indiscipline and vulnerability to counter-attacks. A third successive defeat by Luis Enrique's PSG will sting, but Barcelona return from Paris with reasons to believe they are moving closer to the European champions.

Source: Reuters

MANCHESTER, England, Oct 21 : England's new football regulator has the power to order a club owner to sell and could launch its own investigation once Manchester City's appeal against a verdict that it committed 114 breaches of Premier League financial rules is resolved, its chair David Kogan said. Kogan, chair of the Independent Football Regulator, said it would assess the conduct of owners and senior club officials against its own tests and had the authority to remove an owner if they failed to meet them. "We have the power to ask an owner to step away from a club if we believe that they run a club in a way that is neither fit, fair or done with propriety," Kogan told The Rest Is Football podcast. Asked by co-host Alastair Campbell whether an owner could refuse, Kogan said: "No, no, no. We've got absolute power to do so."

The Independent Football Regulator was established in July 2025 to safeguard the financial sustainability of English football, with powers to oversee club owners and directors and intervene when clubs are at financial risk. The regulator's powers have come into focus amid Manchester City's appeal against the verdict. Kogan said the regulator would wait for that process to play out before deciding whether to mount a separate investigation. "I am not going to get pushed into making any judgement on this until we've seen all of those questions being answered and then we will have to decide whether we're going to mount our own investigation and come to a conclusion on that and what we're going to do," he said. "And pre-empting that would be a colossal mistake." Kogan said the regulator's role differed from the league's because its focus would be on the individuals running clubs rather than imposing sporting sanctions on the clubs themselves. "We would judge against the tests of ownership and senior directors and executives. We would judge the actions of those individuals," he said. "We're not there, we can't, unlike the Premier League, who obviously can take action against the club in terms of fines or points deduction or whatever it may be." Kogan also said the regulator could not automatically prevent a state-backed takeover of an English club under the legislation establishing it. "That legislation does not allow for us to block something just because it's a Norwegian sovereign fund, as an example," he said. "But we're bound very much by the way the legislation has been written, which doesn't preclude that from happening." PREMIER LEAGUE-EFL DEAL In the wide-ranging interview with Gary Lineker and Campbell, Kogan also revealed details of proposals aimed at resolving the long-running dispute over the distribution of money between the Premier League and English Football League. "The Premier League is now talking about more than doubling the amount it pays every year in what are known as solidarity payments, money flowing down to the other (lower) leagues," Kogan said. Under the proposed arrangement, parachute payments to clubs relegated from the Premier League would be reduced while funding flowing into the Championship would increase substantially, Kogan said. He said the changes would narrow the financial gap between relegated clubs receiving parachute payments and their Championship rivals, making the division more competitive. Kogan also questioned the amount being spent on agents, saying fees had surpassed 500 million pounds. "Agents' fees are ridiculous. Over £500 million. It's half a billion pounds," he said. "Hell, I'd much prefer to see it being spent on players." Kogan said another concern was the amount clubs owed one another, which he put at billions of pounds, adding that transfer debt was rising dramatically.

Source: Reuters

LOS ANGELES, Oct 20 : AI data center construction projects, particularly near Dallas/Fort Worth and Washington, DC, are generating new demand for warehouse space and helped send rents higher in the third quarter, real estate services company JLL said on Tuesday. • Companies like Alphabet, Microsoft, Meta and Amazon are spending billions of dollars in a race to dominate artificial intelligence, which requires significant electricity to run servers and computer chips that must be cooled to prevent overheating. • "Data center expansion is driving outsized industrial demand in major freight hubs such as Dallas/Fort Worth, where suppliers and infrastructure providers are clustering near hyperscale campuses," JLL said in its industrial real estate market report for the third quarter. • Average asking rents rose to $10.55 per square foot, up 3.2 per cent from a year earlier, the fastest annual pace of growth since the second quarter of 2024, JLL said.

LIVERPOOL, England, Oct 20 : Rio Ngumoha had already been billed as one of Liverpool's brightest young talents, but on a breathless Champions League night at Anfield on Tuesday the 18-year-old delivered the kind of performance that suggested his time had arrived. With Liverpool trailing by two goals against Villarreal and in desperate need of inspiration, Ngumoha provided it, creating two goals as his side roared back for a dramatic 4-3 victory. "Individually I think I enjoyed myself tonight," Ngumoha said. "As I get older now, affecting games is really important. And today, to get two assists and help the team get the three points, there's nothing more I can ask for." Ngumoha is the youngest Liverpool player to register an assist in the Champions League.

"It's the biggest club in the world, and for me to get that record is something special," he said. "So yeah, I'll take it. I'll take it all day." Looking perfectly at home on one of the game's biggest stages, his first intervention saw him show his composure. With Liverpool having pulled one back through Alexis Mac Allister, Ngumoha produced a delightful dinked pass for Ronald Araujo to haul the hosts level on the brink of halftime. If that offered a glimpse of his talent, what followed after the break felt like a coming-of-age moment. Ngumoha took on Sergi Cardona, skipped past the defender and laid the ball on a plate for Mac Allister to tap Liverpool into the lead for the first time. Supporters at Anfield had spent the opening half-hour watching a Liverpool side stumble from one mistake to another. Suddenly, they were watching an 18-year-old take charge. "On the ball, this kid has so much quality," former Liverpool striker Daniel Sturridge said on the Amazon Prime broadcast. "It is stuff you can't teach. What he does with the ball at his feet, it is God-given ability." Florian Wirtz added a fourth, his first club goal of the season, and although Tani Oluwaseyi's late strike ensured a nervous finish, Liverpool survived to make it three wins from three in Europe. Ngumoha had already made history at Liverpool, becoming the club’s youngest Premier League scorer at Anfield in April, aged 17. He was already the team's youngest scorer thanks to his goal at Newcastle in August 2025 when he was 16. For all the twists in a chaotic seven-goal contest, however, the enduring image was of Ngumoha, and when the final whistle blew supporters celebrated while Duran Duran's "Rio" blasted over the stadium speakers.

BOJ to raise rates to 1.50% in December, sticking to quarterly pace: Reuters poll

TOKYO, Oct 21 : The Bank of Japan will raise interest rates in December to 1.50 per cent, following June and September increases, according to a majority of economists in a Reuters poll, keeping up a quicker pace in a campaign that started with just one rate rise a year. Rising energy and import costs, worsened by a weak yen and the war in the Middle East, are adding to inflation pressure in Japan, and there are more forecasters expecting at least two more rate rises to 2.0 per cent by the middle of next year. A period of relative stability in the yen, which spent most of the year under crushing selling pressure, triggering interventions from the Japanese authorities as well as the US Treasury, also supports the case for a December increase. Last week, board member Junko Koeda said the central bank should not become overly cautious about raising rates, at their highest in 31 years, given the significant upside risks to inflation.

Nearly 70 per cent of economists, 54 of 78, in the October 13-19 survey expected the BOJ to raise its policy rate to 1.5 per cent this quarter, almost double the share in the previous poll. Of the 54 respondents who specified a month, about 80 per cent chose December, while only 2 per cent chose the BOJ's next two-day policy meeting, which concludes on October 30. "With rate hikes in the United States and Europe looking likely before year-end, there is a risk that yen selling could accelerate if the BOJ postpones its move until the new year," said Kazutaka Maeda, senior economist at Meiji Yasuda Research Institute. The BOJ is unlikely to raise rates this month, while the US Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank are expected to raise borrowing costs in December, separate Reuters polls found. "The economy is not overheating to the extent that would warrant consecutive rate hikes, and price developments are also within the BOJ's expected range," said Takeshi Minami, chief economist at Norinchukin Research Institute. Sources have told Reuters many BOJ officials prefer to assess more data on how previous increases have affected financial conditions. RATES TO REACH 2 per cent OR HIGHER Looking into next year, 39 of 65 analysts, or 60 per cent, expected the policy rate to reach 1.75 per cent by end-June, a median unchanged from the September poll. Almost half of 41 respondents who answered an additional question said 1.75 per cent would be the terminal rate. But the share expecting it to reach 2.00 per cent or more rose to 51 per cent, from 40 per cent in September and 36 per cent in August. In September, two board members nominated by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi who support looser fiscal policy opposed the decision to raise rates to 1.25 per cent.  Traders saw the dissent as a sign the BOJ's rate-hike plans could continue to face opposition from Takaichi's administration, briefly pushing the yen lower. Nearly three-quarters of respondents, or 23 of 32, said further dissenting votes when the Policy Board next raises rates could weigh on the yen, which is only about 4 per cent stronger than its 2026 low of around 164 per dollar. "If the dissenting vote were cast in particular by a board member appointed under the Takaichi administration, it could be interpreted as the administration's attempt to restrain rate hikes, potentially heightening concerns that future policy tightening could fall behind the curve," said Kei Fujimoto, senior economist at Sumitomo Mitsui Trust Asset Management. BOND ISSUANCE SEEN BELOW 40 TRILLION YEN Japanese government bond (JGB) yields have risen recently alongside a global market rout, but also on expectations of further BOJ rate hikes and concerns Takaichi's big spending and tax-cut plans will worsen the country's already strained finances. Takaichi has said the government aims to keep new bond issuance at around 40 trillion yen ($251 billion) for the fiscal 2027 budget. She reiterated on Monday Tokyo would "appropriately" control the size of its debt issuance. Nearly two-thirds of economists surveyed, 15 of 23, said new issuance would be kept below 40 trillion yen. "The government is likely keen to increase JGB issuance as a source of funding for growth investment," said Junya Takemoto, senior economist at Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation.  "However, as it becomes more conscious of rising interest rates in the market, it may seek to contain issuance by undertaking a full-scale review of budgets for existing subsidies and funds, ensuring that JGB issuance does not differ markedly from historical levels." Source: Reuters
